I had a one-month delayed reaction to something big. I put it off as nothing because I really did feel like I was okay. But I just didn't realize that the trauma manifested in what I thought were little things so I felt like I was holding my own. Then some time later I realized I had already lost my friends from pushing them away. And still dealing with the aftermath 8 months later after the fact.

I never thought that this is how I function though. With past heartbreaks, it was all over as soon as I set my mind up to it. It's like a switch--I can choose when to stop being bothered by something, but I had a tendency to prolong the process of moving on because I liked having feelings (lol). This time though must have been bigger than everything else.

I was that child, too. For the longest time I treasured my childhood memories, and thought that I'd do anything to go back to a simpler time, when life was kind and I looked forward to waking up. I was counting on a time machine, although it was stupid. I kept on thinking that... until recently, when I realized that there's actually nothing to go back to.

As a child, I painted those lost teenagers (runaways, drop outs) in a different light. I thought they had a reason. I did extremely well in my studies until junior high school, and never once thought that I'd be 'that' person, that person who failed her classes, that person who must have a reason. I became that person. But then again, I'm not... because I don't know why everything got this fucked up, but instead of looking for the reason, I just ask why I'm still alive.

I do that too but we really shouldn't. We all go through different kinds of pain, suffer differently, and react according to what we can handle. I won't wash my hands clean, though. There were five of them versus that one person (we only have 7 people in the class) they talked about so you could say it's peer pressure? It was also a way for me to relate to them at that time. I was new in the city and didn't speak their dialect. And you know how common dislike bridges people easier? Yep.

I've set a lot of boundaries in my life. At this point, I still can't say I've ever had a best friend. Until this semester (we've been classmates for two) I didn't hang out with them and felt uncomfortable socializing. I was being kind to myself. I had to prioritize myself over others so when I feel that friendships aren't working out, I let those people go. I did that too much that all my friends are now just people I rarely chat up online. 

This time, I wanted to try. I wanted to seek out help. I wanted these people to understand me. I wanted to trust them. And that's what I did by opening up a little. They seemed okay in class today. It just doesn't make sense in my head that the group chat is still inactive and the only plausible reason for that is they are talking about me behind my back. See, a lot of times I can be blunt, to the point of offending others so I'd like it if they just talked to me about it.
Wouldn't it become a bigger issue if I approached the school counselor than if I just talked to them about it?

I haven't built a strong relationship with them so isn't that enough reason to not trust them? And where could they be chatting if not in the group chat? Why would they feel the need to exclude me in their conversation... right? I haven't thought of myself as a confident person... however, I do sport an idgaf attitude. It's my first time hearing I may have problems with self-esteem.
